2) Focal (ectopic) atrial tachycardia — regular atrial rate in this range with clear P waves can reflect an ectopic atrial focus producing a sustained tachycardia; P‑wave morphology and consistent atrial rate support this as a close alternate.
3) Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)/paroxysmal SVT (less likely) — usually has abrupt onset/offset and often P waves are not clearly visible or are retrograde; rate here is slower than typical SVT which makes this less likely but it remains possible.
4) Atrial flutter with atypical conduction (less likely) — typical flutter usually shows flutter waves and faster atrial rates (~250–350/min) but atypical flutter with variable conduction can occasionally mimic the observed pattern; consider if P‑wave morphology is abnormal.
5) Sinus tachycardia secondary to systemic causes (anemia, thyrotoxicosis, pulmonary embolism, infection) — not a primary arrhythmia but a common and important cause of sustained sinus tachycardia in pregnancy and must be evaluated because management differs.
